title: Pacer never skips ticks and muxer discards PTS: encoder deficit or dropped frames become ever-growing A/V desync and eventually silent clips
claim: The frame pacer pace() in convert.rs:705-733 never skips ticks: `let due = start + period * index as u32; … if due > now { sleep } else if index > 0 { latest.overruns.fetch_add(1, …) } … index += 1; … let pts = (index as i64 - 1) * 10_000_000 / fps as i64;`. pts is derived purely from the tick index, so when the loop falls behind (encoder submit can block up to 500 ms via `send_timeout(job, SUBMIT_WAIT)` at mft.rs:1184) pts keep advancing 1/fps per frame regardless of wall-clock time. The muxer then throws packet PTS away and muxes the raw ES as CFR with `-f h264 -r fps` (muxer.rs:263), while audio is mapped via `qpc_of = base + pts_us*10` (pipeline.rs:535-537) and the snapshot sets `audio_frames = packets.len()*SR/fps` (pipeline.rs:1002-1003). A sustained encoder deficit or dropped frames therefore become ever-growing A/V desync and eventually silent clips. Overruns are only logged; nothing appears in the UI.
scenario: Encoder sustains 50 fps for a 60 fps config (OBS holding NVENC as in the README's own example, 1440p165, or an iGPU under game load). The loop runs at 50 Hz but pts advance 1/60 s per frame; after 10 minutes the video timeline is about 100 s behind the wall clock. qpc_of() maps packets ~100 s too early, so the audio cut at start_100ns is from long before the picture. Once the lag exceeds the TrackRing (buffer + 2 s), window() returns zeros and the clip is silent; the 'last 30 s' also spans more than 30 s of real time. Every 500 ms submit timeout (a lost frame) shifts everything after it by one frame because the raw ES is muxed at -r fps; audio_frames only fixes the total length. Recordings accumulate both effects over hours.
fix: When now − due > period, set index = elapsed/period (skip ticks) so pts stay true to the wall clock. Mux with real timestamps: a VFR container fed with packet PTS (a minimal NUT/MKV/TS writer piped to ffmpeg), or cut audio per packet at qpc_of(pts). Surface the overrun and drop rate in the UI.

title: Sleep/resume or a long thread stall makes the mixer allocate the whole gap in one window (OOM abort); pacer replays every missed tick
claim: The mixer thread sizes each window from the full elapsed gap with no cap: `let frames = ((target - from) * SAMPLE_RATE as i64 / 10_000_000) as usize; … shared.audio.mix_window(&sources, from, frames, &mut buffers);` (pipeline.rs:780-785), and AudioEngine::mix_window does `track.resize(sample_count, 0.0)` per source plus a scratch buffer of the same size (audio/engine.rs:346-350). After sleep/resume or any long thread stall the whole gap is allocated at once, which is an OOM abort. The pacer likewise replays every missed tick back-to-back. There is no WM_POWERBROADCAST handling anywhere.
scenario: The PC sleeps for an hour with the buffer on; QPC/Instant keep counting across suspend. The first mixer tick after resume (before the 10 s lock-screen stop) asks for ~173M frames, about 1.4 GB of f32 per source plus scratch plus an i16 copy. Allocation fails, the process aborts, the buffer is lost and an in-progress recording loses its BufWriter tail. The pacer replays ~216k missed ticks: encoder at 100% and the ring fills with the pre-sleep still frame under wrong timestamps.
fix: If target − from exceeds about 1 s, account the gap as ring silence and jump from. In the pacer, resync index when more than about 250 ms behind. Stop and restart the pipeline on PBT_APMSUSPEND / resume.

title: NV12 slot reuse is guarded by job count but slots rotate once per conversion, so frames queued for or held by the encoder get overwritten
claim: Latest::submit picks one of SLOTS = 22 NV12 textures round-robin on every WGC conversion: `let slot = self.next_slot; self.next_slot = (self.next_slot + 1) % self.slots.len();` (convert.rs:337-338). The reuse guard counts jobs rather than slots: `*depth as u64 + stats.in_flight.load(..) >= SLOTS as u64` (convert.rs:646, within 643-650; pacer submit path convert.rs:660-681). Because WGC converts on its own thread pool thread independently of the pacer, textures referenced by queued jobs (bounded(4) channel) or held in flight by the encoder can be overwritten with newer pictures, or written while NVENC/AMF reads them. MinUpdateInterval is set best-effort with `let _ = session.SetMinUpdateInterval(interval);` (wgc.rs:208) and the code itself notes it is missing before Windows 11. Off-by-one: the job the pacer holds inside send_timeout is never counted.
scenario: (a) Encoder stall: the pacer blocks up to 500 ms in send_timeout while WGC keeps converting (~30 conversions at 60 Hz); the 22-slot ring laps and the 4 queued jobs and in-flight frames now point at textures holding newer pictures or being written, giving out-of-order or torn frames with every counter clean; the guard only trips at in_flight ≥ 18. (b) High-refresh monitor on Windows 10 (supported per README): WGC delivers 144-240 Hz while the pacer runs at 60, so a job's slot is overwritten about 22/(refresh/fps) ticks later; any encoder holding ~5 or more frames is hit (NVENC lookahead, or AMD with CLIPPIBOY_LOW_LATENCY=0).
fix: Carry the slot index in Job; keep a per-slot refcount; release a slot when the MFT drops the sample (MFCreateTrackedSample + IMFTrackedSample::SetAllocator callback); the converter takes a free slot or skips the frame. Simpler alternative: in the WGC callback only CopyResource into one 'latest BGRA' texture and convert to NV12 in the pacer at tick time, giving one conversion per job and cutting VideoProcessor and watermark GPU work 2-4× at high refresh.

votes.evidence: convert.rs:337-338 `let slot = self.next_slot; self.next_slot = (self.next_slot + 1) % self.slots.len();` advances once per Converter::convert, called from Latest::submit (convert.rs:676) on every WGC FrameArrived (pipeline.rs:684-690 `latest.submit(frame.texture, ...)`, no rate limit in wgc.rs:213-250). The only guard is convert.rs:646 `*depth as u64 + stats.in_flight.load(Ordering::Relaxed) >= SLOTS as u64`, where depth is the channel CAPACITY (mft.rs:1100-1101, set via watch_encoder at pipeline.rs:665), not its occupancy, and in_flight is frames fed minus packets out (mft.rs:1247, 1341). SLOTS = 4+16+2 = 22 (convert.rs:75, mft.rs:37,46), so the guard trips only at in_flight >= 18 and knows nothing about how many conversions happened since a queued/in-flight job took its texture. title: Clip save copies the whole clip (and each WAV) into one Vec, doubling RAM and risking OOM abort with large buffers
claim: muxer::build concatenates the entire clip into one in-memory buffer before writing the temp .h264: `let mut stream: Vec<u8> = Vec::with_capacity(snapshot.packets.iter().map(|p| p.data.len()).sum::<usize>() + …); … std::fs::write(&video_path, &stream)` (muxer.rs:131-141). write_wav (pipeline.rs:238-256) likewise builds the whole WAV in a Vec after window() has already allocated the samples. With the default ring budget of 1.5 × bitrate × seconds (config.rs:100-108) and a buffer slider up to 600 s, a full-length save doubles RAM use.
scenario: At 600 s the ring is ≈3.7 GB at 1440p60 and ≈8.4 GB at 4K60. A full-length save allocates that much again plus ~350 MB transient per audio track at 10 min while a game is running, resulting in an abort or paging that stalls the game.
fix: Stream the header and packets through a BufWriter, or pipe straight into ffmpeg (-f h264 -i pipe:0; stdout/stderr draining already exists). Write WAV samples incrementally (VecDeque::as_slices). Size the budget against GlobalMemoryStatusEx.

votes.reachable_by: A user who has moved the clip folder off the system drive (the default is Videos\ClippiBoy, usually also on C:), when %APPDATA%'s drive has less free space than the snapshot (buffer seconds x bitrate, plus about 11.5 MB/min per WAV track). The existing clip_dir free-space guard would then cover them, but discard_leftovers would have to clear that folder as well. title: COM reference to the video-processor input view leaks on every frame
claim: In convert.rs:336-347, `let input = self.input_view(...)?;` returns a `view.clone()` (an extra COM reference), which is passed as `pInputSurface: std::mem::ManuallyDrop::new(Some(input)),` into the VideoProcessor stream and is never recovered with ManuallyDrop::into_inner / dropped after VideoProcessorBlt. One reference leaks per frame.
scenario: Once a cache entry goes away, the view never dies and keeps its texture and through it the whole ID3D11Device alive. Entries go away on pool Recreate (window or resolution change), watermark toggle, more than 4 entries, or the Converter drop at every pipeline restart. Restarts are frequent (per-game buffer automation, lock screen, screen drift, config changes); each leaks 1-2 frame-sized BGRA textures (8 MB at 1080p, 33 MB at 4K) plus a D3D device. Dragging a window edge during window capture leaks two textures per size step; a long-running tray app grows VRAM steadily.

Nothing calls ManuallyDrop::into_inner/take on stream.pInputSurface, and ManuallyDrop has no drop glue, so one AddRef leaks on every frame, on the success path and the error path alike. The same repo shows the correct pattern in mft.rs:1009-1010 (`ManuallyDrop::take(&mut data.pSample)`), and convert.rs is the only place that misses it. Reachability: wgc.rs FrameArrived handler -> pipeline.rs:678 `latest.submit(frame.texture, ...)` -> convert.rs:676 `self.converter.lock().convert(source, source_size)` runs for every captured frame (Latest::submit skips it only when slots are starved). The cache gets evicted at convert.rs:322-325 (source_size change after wgc.rs:233 `pool.Recreate` on a window or resolution change), at convert.rs:314-317 (watermark switched off), at convert.rs:278-280 (more than 4 entries), and when the Converter is dropped at each pipeline stop or restart (Pipeline::start creates a fresh GpuDevice and Converter per launch: pipeline.rs:625-626, state.rs:497).
votes.reachable_by: Ordinary use, with no attacker needed. The leak of one reference per frame starts as soon as the replay buffer captures (often from startup). Real memory is only lost when a cache entry or the Converter is let go: each buffer stop/start (UI, tray, hotkey, Stream Deck, automation, updater), each resolution change, each watermark toggle, and each window resize in window-capture mode. Monitor capture is the default (config.rs:28), so for most users growth is per restart or resolution change: about 2x8 MB at 1080p without the watermark (both pool textures), or the one canvas texture with it. Each restart also pins the old D3D11 device, because D3D11 child objects hold an internal device reference (runtime behaviour, expected but not checkable here). Window capture with a drag-resize can leak a lot quickly.
votes.fix_assessment: The fix works. Bind the stream mutably and call `drop(ManuallyDrop::take(&mut stream.pInputSurface))` (or into_inner) after VideoProcessorBlt and before the `?`, so the error path is covered too. Another option is to pass a borrowed pointer with transmute_copy and no clone, so the cache stays the only owner.

votes.evidence: convert.rs:260-261 cache hit `return Ok(view.clone());` and convert.rs:289-290 cache miss `self.input_views.push((key, view.clone())); Ok(view)` - either way the caller gets an owned reference beyond the cache's own. convert.rs:336 `let input = self.input_view(...)?;` moves it into convert.rs:347 `pInputSurface: std::mem::ManuallyDrop::new(Some(input)),`; convert.rs:354-360 `VideoProcessorBlt(&self.processor, &self.slots[slot].output_view, 0, &[stream])` borrows a temporary array that is dropped without ManuallyDrop::take/drop, and nothing after it (convert.rs:362-363) gets the reference back. ManuallyDrop never runs the inner Release, so each convert() leaks one AddRef on the current input view. The same codebase does it right elsewhere: mft.rs:1009-1010 `ManuallyDrop::take(&mut data.pSample)` / `ManuallyDrop::take(&mut data.pEvents)`. Eviction paths that make the leak real in memory: convert.rs:304-307 (source_size change), :325-327 (watermark off -> stamp.release()), :287-288 (>=4 entries), and Converter drop on each pipeline start (pipeline.rs:625-626 creates a fresh `GpuDevice::new` + `Converter::new` per start). WGC pool has 2 buffers (wgc.rs:189-193, Recreate at wgc.rs:233-238), so 1 canvas view (watermark on, convert.rs:529-541) or up to 2 pool-texture views (watermark off) are pinned per eviction.
votes.reachable_by: Every captured frame in normal recording. The VRAM leak shows up whenever cached views are evicted: a window or resolution change (pool Recreate plus the source_size clear), switching the watermark off, the 4-entry cap, and every pipeline stop/restart (Converter dropped, GpuDevice recreated). votes.fix_assessment: Either fix works: bind the stream to a mutable local and call `ManuallyDrop::drop(&mut stream.pInputSurface)` (or `ManuallyDrop::into_inner`/`take`) after VideoProcessorBlt, including on the error path, or pass a borrowed pointer with `std::mem::transmute_copy(&input)` and no extra ref. The take-after-call form matches the existing pattern in mft.rs:1009.

The stream is moved into the array temporary and never unwrapped; windows 0.58 (Cargo.toml:65) generates no Drop for D3D11_VIDEO_PROCESSOR_STREAM, which is why the field is ManuallyDrop. So one Release is missed per converted frame, on the success path and the error path alike. What gets pinned: the watermark is on by default (watermark.rs:34 `ENABLED: AtomicBool = AtomicBool::new(true)`), so the view is normally on the Stamp canvas (convert.rs:336 `stamped.as_ref().unwrap_or(source)`), one source-sized BGRA texture. With the watermark off, the views are on the 2 WGC pool buffers (wgc.rs:189-193, `2`). The cache drops entries on a size change (convert.rs:326-329), on a watermark toggle (convert.rs:345-347 region, `stamp.release()` then clear), and on Converter drop. Each pipeline start builds a fresh device (pipeline.rs:625 `GpuDevice::new`). Restarts come from game-start/stop automation (lib.rs:661-662), the lock screen, screen drift (lib.rs:587-588) and source changes (commands.rs:119-120). Pool Recreate on every content-size change: wgc.rs:226-240.
votes.corrected_claim: The leak itself is real. What leaks is not memory per frame: the refcount of the same few cached views keeps rising, and those view objects can never be freed. The memory lost is one set of textures per cache lifetime. With the default watermark on, that is about 1 canvas texture per pipeline restart, per settled resize, or per watermark-off toggle. With the watermark off, it is the 2 pool buffers. Each set also likely pins the old ID3D11Device through D3D11's child-to-device internal reference (runtime behaviour, not checkable here). The cache clear at more than 4 entries almost never happens in practice. Typical growth is about 8 MB at 1080p or 33 MB at 4K per restart, plus the device. Because `&[stream]` moves the struct, bind it first: `let streams = [stream]; let result = unsafe { ...VideoProcessorBlt(..., &streams) }; let [stream] = streams; drop(std::mem::ManuallyDrop::into_inner(stream.pInputSurface)); result.map_err(...)?;`. Releasing right after Blt is safe because the D3D11 runtime tracks in-flight use itself. Once views can die, the existing size/toggle cache clears start freeing textures as their comments intend. Cached entries still hold strong refs, so the raw-pointer key cannot alias while it is in the table.

title: Refresh-rate snapping produces 59 fps on 59.94 Hz panels
claim: The refresh rate comes from integer dmDisplayFrequency (capture.rs:155-158) and `choices.push(refresh)` adds it as an fps step (capture.rs:598-606), so fractional rates are truncated.
scenario: A 59.94 Hz panel reports 59, so a 60 fps config snaps to 59 fps CFR; the pacer then misses about one WGC frame per second (judder). Same at 119/143/164 Hz.
fix: Treat ±1 Hz around a standard step as that step, or read the rational refresh rate from QueryDisplayConfig.

votes.evidence: capture.rs:155-158 `match mode.dmDisplayFrequency { 0 | 1 => None, hz => Some(hz) }` (integer from EnumDisplaySettingsW, used as-is). capture.rs:598-605 fps_choices: `STEPS.into_iter().filter(|fps| *fps < refresh)` then `choices.push(refresh)`, so refresh=59 gives [30, 59]. capture.rs:610-619 snap_fps(60, [30,59]) finds the highest step <= 60, which is 59. capture.rs:641 `recording.fps = snap_fps(...)`, and state.rs:496 applies fit_to_target before Pipeline::start. convert.rs:694-733 pace() ticks at `1_000_000_000 / fps` ns and samples the latest WGC frame, so at 59 ticks/s against a 59.94 Hz source about 0.94 source frames per second are never sampled. The UI mirrors this (src/routes/Recording.tsx fpsChoices/fitFps). The input condition rests on Windows: legacy DEVMODE reports a 59.94 Hz (TV/NTSC-style) mode as 59, and 119.88 as 119. That is documented Windows behaviour but cannot be checked from source; for typical PC '60 Hz' panels Windows usually reports 60.
votes.reachable_by: Any user whose capture screen runs a fractional mode that Windows reports truncated (59.94 -> 59, 119.88 -> 119): TVs, some laptop or HDMI modes. A saved 60/120 fps config is snapped down at every pipeline launch, and the UI offers only the truncated value.
votes.fix_assessment: Sound. Treating refresh within about 1 Hz below a standard step (59 -> 60, 119 -> 120, 143 -> 144) as that step, or reading the rational vSyncFreq from QueryDisplayConfig (which the code already calls for identities), fixes both fps_choices and the UI mirror. Recording.tsx must be changed in step.

title: Encoder thread polls instead of blocking
claim: The encoder loop uses `jobs.recv_timeout(2ms)` (mft.rs:1330), `sleep(1ms)` (mft.rs:1354), and a busy-polling drain loop (mft.rs:1406-1411) around GetEvent(NO_WAIT).
scenario: 500-1000 wakeups per second. crossbeam's timed park may round up to the 15.6 ms system timer, so HaveOutput events can wait.
fix: A helper thread doing a blocking GetEvent(0) and forwarding into a crossbeam channel, then select! over events and jobs (or BeginGetEvent).

votes.evidence: mft.rs:1328-1330 `if pending_input > 0 { match jobs.recv_timeout(Duration::from_millis(2))`. mft.rs:1351-1354 `} else if !handled { std::thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(1)); }`. mft.rs:1281 drains with `events.GetEvent(MF_EVENT_FLAG_NO_WAIT)`. crossbeam-channel-0.5.16/src/context.rs:153 `thread::park_timeout(end - now)` is the timed wait, and a send unparks it at once, but MF events do not. So the thread wakes every 1-2 ms (or at system-timer granularity) whenever the encoder is idle, and a HaveOutput event that arrives during a recv wait is seen only at the timeout or the next job (at most about one frame period). Nuance: the loop at mft.rs:1404-1411 is the stop-time drain only (bounded to 2 s) and sleeps 1 ms per empty poll, so it is not a steady-state busy spin. The 15.6 ms rounding of park_timeout rests on Windows timer resolution and std's WaitOnAddress timeout, which cannot be checked here (no std or windows sources locally).
votes.reachable_by: Every running hardware-encoder pipeline (always async), continuously while buffering.
votes.fix_assessment: Reasonable. BeginGetEvent with an IMFAsyncCallback forwarding into a crossbeam channel, plus select! over events and jobs, removes the polling. A helper thread on blocking GetEvent(0) also works but needs a clean shutdown (MFShutdownObject / IMFShutdown) so it does not block forever at stop.

title: Encoder thread never initialises COM
claim: On the clippiboy-encoder thread (mft.rs:1115-1131), MFStartup, MFTEnumEx and ActivateObject run without CoInitializeEx. This only works because other threads (audio ensure_com, windows-rs CoIncrementMTAUsage) keep the implicit MTA alive.
scenario: If no other thread keeps the implicit MTA alive, MF/COM calls on the encoder thread run without COM initialised.
fix: Call CoInitializeEx(MTA) at thread start.

votes.evidence: mft.rs:1112-1130: the clippiboy-encoder thread closure calls `build(&gpu, &settings)` and then `run(...)` directly. build (mft.rs:681-717) calls `startup()` (MFStartup, mft.rs:149-157, once per process), `enumerate()` (MFTEnumEx) and `candidates[pick].activate.ActivateObject()` (CoCreateInstance of the vendor MFT). A grep of src-tauri/src finds CoInitializeEx only in audio/capture.rs:471 and audio/devices.rs:33 (ensure_com), never on the encoder thread, and no CoUninitialize anywhere. So the encoder thread relies on the implicit MTA that other MTA threads in the process create (audio capture threads, ensure_com callers, possibly MF's own work-queue threads after MFStartup, or windows-rs's CO_E_NOTINITIALIZED -> CoIncrementMTAUsage fallback). The last two cannot be verified here because no windows-rs or MF sources are local.
votes.reachable_by: Theoretical: a pipeline start where no other thread has created the process MTA yet. This is most plausible on the first start with no audio sources enabled, since encoder build runs before wgc::start (pipeline.rs:629-659 vs 666). Then ActivateObject or CoCreateInstance would fail with CO_E_NOTINITIALIZED.
votes.fix_assessment: Correct and cheap: CoInitializeEx(None, COINIT_MULTITHREADED) at the top of the encoder thread closure. Ideally pair it with CoUninitialize after the Transform and the event generator are dropped at the end of run().

title: Mixer timeline truncates per window, so long recordings drift
claim: pipeline.rs:818 is `next_100ns = Some(from + frames as i64 * 10_000_000 / SAMPLE_RATE as i64);`, which floors away 1/3 to 2/3 of a 100 ns tick per window.
scenario: The recorder's contiguous PCM drifts behind the video by about 12 ms per hour. The replay ring's trimming cancels the error, so clips are unaffected.
fix: Keep an origin plus a u64 sample counter.

also.title: Mixer `next_100ns` truncation accumulates timing drift
also.claim: The mixer advances its window with `next_100ns = from + frames*1e7/48000` (pipeline.rs:818), which truncates each step and accumulates about 3.5 ppm of drift.
also.fix: Derive it from a total frame count instead.

votes.evidence: pipeline.rs:818 `next_100ns = Some(from + frames as i64 * 10_000_000 / SAMPLE_RATE as i64);` -> frames*625/3 integer division drops (frames mod 3)/3 of a tick per window (avg ~1/3 tick = 33 ns). pipeline.rs:780 `frames = ((target - from) * SAMPLE_RATE as i64 / 10_000_000)` makes the next window catch up to the clock, so the sample count grows faster than QPC time. MIX_INTERVAL = 10 ms (pipeline.rs:44), so ~100 windows/s -> ~12 ms/h (~3.3 ppm). Sources are read by QPC each window (engine.rs:392 `run.ring.read_window(from_100ns, scratch)`), so the overlap shows up as repeated samples. The recorder counts samples contiguously (recorder.rs:293 `track.frames += ...`, :301 `audio.timeline += frames`) and finalize only cuts the tail to the video length (recorder.rs:546 `audio_frames = frames * SAMPLE_RATE / fps`, align at :439), so audio lags the CFR video more and more. The comment at pipeline.rs:761-762 ('no error can build up') is wrong. Replay ring: the trim at pipeline.rs:165 `inner.start_100ns += frames * 10_000_000 / SAMPLE_RATE as i64` uses the same floor on the same per-window chunk once the ring is full, so the two errors cancel.
votes.corrected_claim: Small nuance on the side claim: the replay ring cancels the error only while windows are trimmed one by one. Silent or muted windows are counted but not stored (pipeline.rs:120-138). When sound returns they are trimmed together with the block as one chunk, so for sources with digital silence a small residual drift builds up in clips too, until silence longer than the ring resets it.
votes.reachable_by: Any long recording (Recorder path). After about an hour the offset is ~8-12 ms, depending on how often the mixer actually wakes. The replay ring is mostly unaffected.
votes.fix_assessment: An origin plus a cumulative frame counter (next = origin + total_frames*1e7/48000) fixes the mixer. The TrackRing trim at pipeline.rs:165 has the same truncation and today cancels the mixer error. Fixing only line 818 would move the drift into clips (ring start falls behind over buffer uptime, so audio comes out early), so the trim has to switch to a cumulative trimmed-frame counter too.

title: Pipeline stop order contradicts its own comment (capture dropped after encoder)
claim: The field comment (pipeline.rs:577-578) says the capture 'Has to drop before the encoder', but stop() (pipeline.rs:746-750) drops the encoder explicitly first and `_capture` only goes when the function returns.
scenario: WGC keeps converting and watermarking into slots throughout the ≤2 s encoder drain.
fix: Take and drop the capture first.

votes.evidence: pipeline.rs:577-578 `/// Has to drop before the encoder: no frame may arrive after that.` `_capture: Capture,`. In stop() (pipeline.rs:735-751): latest.stop(); pacer.join(); mixer.join(); `if let Some(encoder) = running.encoder.take() { drop(encoder); }`, and `running`, with `_capture`, only drops when the function returns. drop(encoder) is the last Arc (the sink's clone dropped with the pacer). VideoEncoder::drop joins the thread (mft.rs:1211-1216), and that thread drains for up to 2 s (mft.rs:1405 `Duration::from_secs(2)`). Meanwhile the WGC callback (pipeline.rs:676-684) keeps calling latest.submit, which does not check `running` (convert.rs:660-680) and converts into an NV12 slot, watermark included (convert.rs:317). Capture::drop (wgc.rs:66-72) removes the handler only afterwards.
votes.reachable_by: Every pipeline stop (buffer off, app exit through Pipeline::drop). The only cost is wasted GPU conversion during the drain. Latest/Converter outlive the encoder and the slot guard (convert.rs:641-648) still applies, so there is no corruption.
votes.fix_assessment: Make `_capture` an Option and take()/drop it at the top of stop() (or right after the pacer join). That matches the comment and costs at most a few repeated tail frames from the pacer.

title: 22 NV12 slots allocated up front waste VRAM (S4)
claim: All SLOTS = 22 NV12 textures are allocated up front: about 68 MB at 1080p, 122 MB at 1440p and 273 MB at 4K of VRAM, even with a near-zero queue.
scenario: Hundreds of MB of VRAM held while gaming at 4K.
fix: Not given explicitly here (see proposal: adaptive slot pool grown on demand using tracked samples).

votes.evidence: convert.rs:75 `pub const SLOTS: usize = crate::mft::QUEUE_DEPTH + crate::mft::ENCODER_HOLD_MAX + 2;` with mft.rs:37 `QUEUE_DEPTH: usize = 4` and mft.rs:46 `ENCODER_HOLD_MAX: usize = 16` -> 22. convert.rs:170-178 `for _ in 0..SLOTS { slots.push(Self::make_slot(... width, height)?) }` allocates every slot in Converter::new (called once at pipeline.rs:626 with recording.width/height); make_slot convert.rs:213-226 creates a DXGI_FORMAT_NV12, D3D11_USAGE_DEFAULT texture. Rotation is strict round-robin (convert.rs:337-338 `self.next_slot = (self.next_slot + 1) % self.slots.len();`), so all 22 are touched and stay resident. Numbers check: w*h*1.5 x 22 = 68.4 MB (1080p), 121.7 MB (1440p), 273.7 MB (2160p), plus driver pitch alignment. 2160 is a UI choice (src/routes/Recording.tsx:14 `HEIGHTS = [720, 1080, 1440, 2160]`), height clamped to the source (capture.rs:646), width follows aspect, so ultrawide 5120x2160 is ~365 MB. The comment at convert.rs:70-73 itself concedes 'the headroom mostly goes unused' because low_latency_default (mft.rs:433-437) keeps AMD/Intel queues near zero.
votes.reachable_by: Every buffer/recording session; cost scales with the configured output resolution (4K or ultrawide sources at native height are the expensive cases).
votes.fix_assessment: An on-demand pool is feasible because the in-flight count and real queue depth are already tracked (convert.rs:641-649), but growth must happen before the rotation laps the encoder or it reintroduces the torn-frame bug convert.rs:62-68 describes; a simpler middle ground is sizing from the effective low-latency/vendor setting or using a free list instead of strict round-robin. This is a deliberate, documented trade-off, so the priority is low.

title: Screenshot path creates a new D3D device per screenshot
claim: shot.rs:516 creates a new D3D device for every screenshot grab().
scenario: Each screenshot pays device creation cost.
fix: Not given explicitly in the report (implied: reuse a device).

votes.evidence: shot.rs:516 `let gpu = Arc::new(crate::gpu::GpuDevice::new(None)?);` inside grab(), called once per take_screenshot (state.rs:902). GpuDevice::new runs D3D11CreateDevice (gpu.rs:202-220), SetMultithreadProtected, and CreateDirect3D11DeviceFromDXGIDevice for the WinRT device (gpu.rs:237-243) every time. Nothing caches it.

title: mft::run is ~225 lines and duplicates event handling in the drain loop
claim: mft::run is about 225 lines long and duplicates the MFT event handling in the drain loop.
scenario: Fixes to event handling must be made twice and can diverge.
fix: Not given explicitly in the report (implied: factor out shared event handling).

votes.evidence: src-tauri/src/mft.rs:1221 `fn run<F, H>(` through the closing `}` at 1445 (after `ProcessMessage(MFT_MESSAGE_NOTIFY_END_STREAMING, 0)` at 1443): exactly 225 lines. Main loop 1278-1320: `events.GetEvent(MF_EVENT_FLAG_NO_WAIT)` / `MF_E_NO_EVENTS_AVAILABLE => break` / `kind == METransformHaveOutput` -> `transform.take_output(duration)` -> `took(...)`, `on_packet(packet)`, `catch_up_on_header(...)` / `METransformDrainComplete` -> finished. Drain loop 1399-1431 repeats the same dispatch: `GetEvent(MF_EVENT_FLAG_NO_WAIT)` ... `if kind == METransformHaveOutput.0 as u32 { match transform.take_output(duration) { Ok(Some(packet)) => on_packet(packet), ... Err(err) => { log::warn!("{err}"); break; } } } else if kind == METransformDrainComplete.0 as u32 { break; }`. The software branch (1368-1385) repeats the take_output -> took -> on_packet -> catch_up_on_header sequence a third time.

The drain-loop copy is a cut-down version and already differs from the main loop: it skips `took` (so drained frames never reach the encoder stats), skips `catch_up_on_header`, stops on a take_output error where the main loop logs and carries on, and sleeps instead of breaking when no events are waiting. votes.reachable_by: Maintainers only; no runtime trigger. A future fix to the async event dispatch has to be applied to both the main loop and the drain loop.
votes.fix_assessment: Factoring out a `handle_event(kind) -> Flow` helper (or a closure shared by both loops) that covers HaveOutput and DrainComplete would remove the duplication. The drain-specific differences (sleep on no events, 2 s deadline) stay at the call site. Low value, low risk.

title: muxer::run and run_reporting duplicate error formatting
claim: muxer::run and muxer::run_reporting duplicate the ffmpeg error formatting.

title: frames*SR/fps audio-length formula is duplicated
claim: The `frames*SR/fps` formula for audio length appears twice (pipeline.rs:1002 and recorder.rs:546).
scenario: Clip and recording audio alignment can diverge if one copy changes.
fix: Not given explicitly in the report (implied: one shared helper).

votes.corrected_claim: Accurate but trivial. It is a one-line formula in two places, with different integer types (i64 vs u64). Both copies guard fps with `.max(1)` and agree today. Neighbouring 100ns<->sample-frame conversions (pipeline.rs:165, 181, 780, 818, 1049; recorder.rs:265) are repeated inline in the same way.

title: Vestigial EncodedPacket.track / duration_us fields and audio cases in buffer tests

scenario: Dead fields and tests for a code path that no longer exists.
fix: Not given explicitly in the report (implied: remove them).

votes.evidence: The only production constructor is src-tauri/src/mft.rs:1051-1057 `EncodedPacket { track: VIDEO_TRACK, pts_us: ..., duration_us: duration_100ns / 10, ... }`. Strictly, the `track` field is still read (by `is_video()`), but in production it only ever holds VIDEO_TRACK, so the reads are no-ops. `duration_us` is written and never read. The audio packets in the test `fill` helper exercise a situation the pipeline can no longer produce (audio goes to TrackRings, not the ReplayBuffer). votes.reachable_by: Nothing at runtime; it is dead weight in data (16 bytes per packet) and tests.
votes.fix_assessment: Removing `track`, `duration_us`, `VIDEO_TRACK`, `is_video()` and the audio pushes in `fill` is safe. title: The last ~80 ms of every clip is silent
claim: The mixer runs `AUDIO_LAG_100NS = 80ms` behind QPC now (pipeline.rs:42), and Pipeline::snapshot (pipeline.rs:983-1026) doesn't wait for the mixer to catch up, so window() fills the clip tail with zeros (80 ms minus encoder latency).
scenario: Every saved clip ends with a short stretch of silence.
fix: Wait up to ~100 ms for the mixer horizon to pass the clip end, or trim the trailing packets.

votes.evidence: pipeline.rs:42 `const AUDIO_LAG_100NS: i64 = 80 * 10_000;`. pipeline.rs:775 `let target = now_100ns() - AUDIO_LAG_100NS;` with MIX_INTERVAL 10 ms (pipeline.rs:45). snapshot (pipeline.rs:983-1026) takes packets up to the newest one and sets `audio_frames = packets.len() * SAMPLE_RATE / fps` from `start_100ns = qpc_of(first_pts)`, with no wait on the mixer. state.rs:822-824 says 'There is nothing to wait for'. TrackRing::window (pipeline.rs:175-200) leaves zeros wherever `inner.samples.get(src)` is None. BUT ClipSnapshot.tracks is `self.shared.tracks.lock().clone()`, a Vec<Arc<TrackRing>> of the live rings, not a copy (pipeline.rs:545, 1019). The window is read only inside muxer::build at muxer.rs:172/190, after it builds the whole elementary stream and `std::fs::write(&video_path, &stream)` (muxer.rs:131-141), plus game_for and destination in state.rs:843-845. The mixer keeps filling the rings during that time.
votes.corrected_claim: A real trailing-silence defect exists, but it is not a fixed ~80 ms on every clip. At snapshot time the rings lag the clip end by roughly 80 ms plus up to 10 ms mixer tick, minus the encoder/pacer latency. The audio window is read later from the live rings, after muxer::build has assembled and written the whole .h264 file. So the silent tail is that lag minus the save-path time before the WAV write. It is typically some tens of ms on short clips and can be zero on long or high-bitrate clips whose video write takes longer than the lag.
votes.reachable_by: Every buffered clip save (hotkey, tray, UI, Stream Deck), and most visibly short clips on fast disks. Recordings via Recorder are a different path.
votes.fix_assessment: Waiting in save_clip, after releasing the pipeline lock, until a mixer horizon atomic (next_100ns, not exposed today) passes start_100ns + audio_frames, with a ~150 ms cap, fixes it deterministically. Trimming the last few video packets also works but shortens the clip.

title: convert.rs is #![cfg(windows)], so pure pacer and slot logic can't be tested
claim: convert.rs is `#![cfg(windows)]`, so the pure pacer and slot logic inside it cannot be unit-tested (on non-Windows CI).
scenario: Bugs like VP-1 and VP-2 in pacer/slot logic have no test coverage.
fix: Not given explicitly in the report (implied: move pure logic out of the cfg(windows) module and test it).

votes.evidence: src-tauri/src/convert.rs:16 `#![cfg(windows)]`; convert.rs has no #[cfg(test)]/#[test] at all (grep empty). But mft.rs:12 is also `#![cfg(windows)]` and still carries tests (mft.rs:1447 `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` ... `fn an_idr_opens_a_gop`), so the cfg gate does not stop tests on Windows. The real coupling: `pub struct Latest { converter: Mutex<Converter>, ... encoder: Mutex<Option<(Arc<crate::mft::EncoderStats>, usize)>> }` (convert.rs:581-612), `fn on_frame(&mut self, texture: &ID3D11Texture2D, ...)` (convert.rs:577), `pace()` does `latest.converter.lock(); converter.texture(slot as usize).clone()` (convert.rs:727-729); slot rotation `self.next_slot = (self.next_slot + 1) % self.slots.len()` sits inside Converter::convert next to D3D11 video-processor calls (convert.rs:337-338). The obstacle is not the #![cfg(windows)] gate alone (mft.rs is gated the same way and has tests that run under cargo test on Windows) but that the pacer timing math and slot bookkeeping are fused with D3D11 objects (Latest owns a Converter that needs a real ID3D11Device; FrameSink takes &ID3D11Texture2D; slot rotation lives inside Converter::convert), so they cannot be exercised without a GPU on any platform; and no CI job runs cargo test anyway (see VP-39).
votes.reachable_by: Developers/CI only; regressions in pace() (index/pts math, overrun counting) or slot_would_be_snatched go uncaught.
votes.fix_assessment: Extracting the tick schedule (due time, pts, duplicate/overrun decisions) and the slot-availability rule into plain functions/structs without D3D types would make them testable on every platform; it only helps if some CI job then actually runs cargo test.

title: B-frames with raw Annex-B remux at -r, pts-filtered snapshot and discarded PTS is fragile (S5)
claim: B-frames (enabled via CLIPPIBOY_BFRAMES or a driver default) combined with raw Annex-B remux at -r fps, a pts-filtered snapshot and discarded PTS is fragile.
scenario: With reordered frames, snapshot cut points and CFR remux may produce misordered or broken output.
fix: Not given explicitly in the report.

votes.evidence: B-frames: mft.rs:392-400 `let count = env_opt_u32("CLIPPIBOY_BFRAMES")?; ... CODECAPI_AVEncMPVDefaultBPictureCount` (otherwise not set; README.md:648 'unset means the driver's own choice, which is what ships'). Mux: muxer.rs:138-143 concatenates raw packet bytes into clip_*.h264; muxer.rs:261-263 `// The elementary stream carries no timestamps — the frame rate supplies them.` `command.arg("-f").arg("h264").arg("-r").arg(fps...)` with `-c:v copy` (muxer.rs:296); same path for recordings (recorder.rs:433, 595). PTS: mft.rs:1032 `let pts_100ns = sample.GetSampleTime()` is the only timestamp read; no MFSampleExtension_DecodeTimestamp anywhere, and pts_us is used only for the ring/audio anchor. Snapshot: buffer.rs:197 `.filter(|p| p.pts_us >= start_pts)`. But keyframes are IDR/SPS (mft.rs:935 `matches!(header & 0x1f, 5 | 7)`, mft.rs:1031 CleanPoint), and with closed GOPs nothing before an IDR in decode order has pts >= the IDR's, so the filter selects exactly a seq cut; the first packet is the GOP's minimum pts, so the audio anchor (pipeline.rs:989) is right, and audio length comes from packet count (pipeline.rs:1004), which reordering does not change. The mft.rs:1259 comment shows the author already knew output can arrive reordered.
votes.corrected_claim: Only the remux step is fragile. With B-frames on (opt-in through CLIPPIBOY_BFRAMES, or whatever the driver defaults to, mainly NVENC, which runs without low latency per mft.rs:433-437), the MP4 timestamps depend entirely on ffmpeg rebuilding presentation order from a raw Annex-B stream under -c copy, because the encoder's PTS/DTS never reach the mux. Without picture-timing SEI this commonly gives unset or pts==dts timestamps, so frames play in decode order (judder). That rests on ffmpeg behaviour that cannot be checked here. The pts-filtered snapshot is not itself broken by reordering: with closed IDR GOPs it is the same as a sequence cut, and with open GOPs it only drops leading pictures that could not be decoded anyway.
votes.reachable_by: A user or tester who sets CLIPPIBOY_BFRAMES>0, or a GPU driver whose H.264 MFT emits B-frames by default (unknown; AMF/QSV run in low-latency mode, which typically suppresses them).
votes.fix_assessment: Cheapest robust fix: explicitly set AVEncMPVDefaultBPictureCount=0 unless the env var asks otherwise, which removes the dependency on ffmpeg's raw-stream timestamp guessing. Supporting B-frames properly would mean carrying the encoder's PTS (and DTS) into the mux, for example a timestamped intermediate container, instead of a bare elementary stream with -r.

title: Screenshot read_back runs for every arriving frame, not just the first
claim: shot.rs:531-533 is `let _ = sender.try_send(read_back(&gpu, frame.texture));`, so the staging copy, a blocking Map and a 24 MB (4K) conversion run for every frame that arrives before the capture is dropped, even though only the first result can be sent.
scenario: Several full read-backs and conversions per screenshot at 4K.
fix: Check whether the channel is already full before calling read_back.

votes.evidence: shot.rs:531-533 `move |frame| { let _ = sender.try_send(read_back(&gpu, frame.texture)); }`: read_back (staging CreateTexture2D, CopyResource, blocking Map, BGRA->RGB loop, shot.rs:566-620) runs before the channel is looked at. Bounds: the frame pool has 2 buffers (wgc.rs:189-194, `2`), callbacks are serialized by `Mutex::new(on_frame)` (wgc.rs:213, :251), and grab drops the capture as soon as recv returns (shot.rs:543-548). Capture::drop does RemoveFrameArrived/Close (wgc.rs:66-72). Also, the bounded(1) channel is emptied by `receiver.recv_timeout`, so a later frame does not find it full (the comment at shot.rs:517-518 is inaccurate).
votes.corrected_claim: The waste is real but bounded. Typically at most one extra read-back: a frame WGC wrote into the second pool buffer while the first was being converted, and only on a changing screen or a moving cursor (cursor capture is on). It runs on the callback thread after grab() has already returned the shot, so it does not delay the screenshot. It costs an extra ~25 MB transient allocation and some CPU/GPU time at 4K. 'Several' read-backs per screenshot is overstated.
votes.reachable_by: Screenshots of a source that redraws (game, video, cursor movement) at high resolution.
votes.fix_assessment: The proposed 'check whether the channel is full' does not work reliably: once the main thread has received, the bounded(1) channel is empty again, so later callbacks still run read_back. An AtomicBool claimed with swap(true) before read_back (or dropping the sender after the first send) is the robust fix.

title: Async MF_E_TRANSFORM_STREAM_CHANGE handling consumes the HaveOutput event without retrying and never re-reads SPS/PPS
claim: On MF_E_TRANSFORM_STREAM_CHANGE (mft.rs:1015-1023) the code sets the new output type then does `return Ok(None)`, consuming the METransformHaveOutput event without calling ProcessOutput again. The SPS/PPS header is never re-read afterwards because catch_up_on_header (mft.rs:896-911) stops at the first non-empty header.
scenario: One packet is delayed or stuck, in-flight pairing is off by one, and a stale header may be prepended to clips.
fix: Call ProcessOutput again immediately; re-read the header; as a fallback extract SPS/PPS (NAL 7/8) from the first IDR packet.

votes.evidence: mft.rs:1015-1023: on MF_E_TRANSFORM_STREAM_CHANGE it calls `GetOutputAvailableType(0,0)` and `SetOutputType`, then `return Ok(None);`. mft.rs:1307-1323: the METransformHaveOutput branch treats Ok(None) as a no-op, with no retry and no `sent.pop_front()`. mft.rs:896-911 catch_up_on_header: `if !*pending { return; }` and `*pending = false` once a non-empty header is read, and nothing ever sets it back to true. However, catch_up_on_header runs only after a packet has been delivered (mft.rs:1314-1319), so for the change 'once at the beginning' the comment describes (before the first packet), the header is read from the post-change current type. A stale header needs a mid-stream type change after a header was already captured, or a non-empty setup header (mft.rs:1238). muxer.rs:137 prepends the header once, and encoders that write SPS/PPS inline before IDRs override it. The sync path (mft.rs:1362-1391) is effectively dead: the software MFT fails at MFT_MESSAGE_SET_D3D_MANAGER (mft.rs:742-755).
votes.corrected_claim: The code does consume the HaveOutput event and return without a retry, and the header chase stops at the first non-empty header. Whether a packet is lost or delayed depends on whether the async MFT sends a fresh METransformHaveOutput after SetOutputType. FFmpeg mfenc, as recalled, also clears async_have_output and waits for a new event in this case. The stale-header case needs a mid-stream output-type change after the header was captured. That is not the start-of-stream change the code targets, and it is harmless when the encoder writes SPS/PPS inline. None of this can be checked from source.
votes.reachable_by: Only a hardware async H.264 MFT (NVENC/AMF/QSV driver) that returns MF_E_TRANSFORM_STREAM_CHANGE and does not re-signal METransformHaveOutput, or one that changes its output type mid-stream after delivering a header and does not repeat SPS/PPS inline.
votes.fix_assessment: Calling ProcessOutput again immediately is risky: an async MFT may reject ProcessOutput without a pending HaveOutput event (E_UNEXPECTED), or give the sample to the retry and then fail on the re-signalled event. Setting header_pending = true after a stream change, and extracting SPS/PPS (NAL 7/8) from the first IDR packet as a fallback, are cheap and safe hardening.

title: MinUpdateInterval equal to the frame period may skip alternate frames (S1)
claim: WGC MinUpdateInterval is set exactly equal to the frame period; because of jitter this may cause WGC to skip alternate frames.
scenario: Delivered frame rate halves intermittently, and the CFR pacer repeats frames.
fix: Since the pacer does CFR anyway, use about 0.5-0.9 × the period.

votes.evidence: src-tauri/src/wgc.rs:205-208 `if fps > 0 { let interval: TimeSpan = Duration::from_nanos(1_000_000_000 / fps as u64).into(); let _ = session.SetMinUpdateInterval(interval); }` - fps is recording.fps (pipeline.rs:671-676 passes `recording.fps`), and capture::fps_choices (capture.rs:598-606) always offers the panel refresh itself, so interval == refresh period is the normal 'source' choice. The value is truncated (integer ns, then 100 ns ticks), i.e. marginally shorter than 1/fps. The pacer (convert.rs:694-733) repeats the last slot on any tick without a new frame and counts it in `duplicated`.
votes.corrected_claim: The code does set MinUpdateInterval to exactly (slightly under, by truncation) one frame period. Whether that halves delivery depends on how WGC/DWM implement the interval (comparing vsync-quantized present times against the last delivered frame with or without tolerance) and on the panel's true refresh (e.g. 60.02 Hz vs nominal 60). If WGC does gate on 'elapsed >= interval', the more likely effect is broader than alternate-frame skips: with fps not a divisor of refresh (60 on 144 Hz, 120 on 165 Hz) delivery would quantize to ceil(interval/vsync) vsyncs (about 48 and 82 fps), and the pacer fills the gap with duplicates. None of this can be checked from source; the call is also a no-op where the API is missing (pre-Windows 11).
votes.reachable_by: Any recording on Windows 11 where SetMinUpdateInterval exists, especially fps == panel refresh or fps not dividing the refresh rate.
votes.fix_assessment: A margin (about 0.5-0.9x period) is cheap since the pacer is CFR anyway, but every extra WGC frame is converted to NV12 and rotates a slot, so it raises converter load and slot churn (relevant to VP-2); verify with the existing `duplicated` counter on real hardware before and after.

title: MFTEnumEx called without adapter LUID; MFT may belong to a different adapter (S2)
claim: MFTEnumEx is called without an adapter LUID, so on same-vendor multi-GPU machines the chosen MFT may belong to a different adapter than the D3D11 device.
scenario: Ryzen APU + AMD dGPU: the encoder MFT is bound to the other adapter than the capture device.
fix: Use MFTEnum2 with the device's adapter LUID.

votes.evidence: src-tauri/src/mft.rs:219-226 `MFTEnumEx(MFT_CATEGORY_VIDEO_ENCODER, MFT_ENUM_FLAG_HARDWARE | MFT_ENUM_FLAG_SYNCMFT | MFT_ENUM_FLAG_SORTANDFILTER, Some(&input), Some(&output), ...)` - no adapter attribute; no LUID/MFTEnum2 anywhere in src-tauri/src (grep empty). Selection is by vendor string only: mft.rs:710-714 `candidates.iter().position(|c| c.id == Some(wanted))` via vendor_of/vendor_to_encoder (mft.rs:159-178, `MFT_ENUM_HARDWARE_VENDOR_ID_Attribute`). The D3D device goes to a different rule: gpu.rs:141-147 picks the same-vendor adapter with max dedicated_vram (comment explicitly names the Ryzen iGPU+dGPU case). The device is handed over with MFT_MESSAGE_SET_D3D_MANAGER (mft.rs:739-757), and an error there aborts with 'device to encoder: ...'.
votes.corrected_claim: Code facts hold: the MFT is chosen by vendor id alone, with no adapter LUID, while the D3D11 device is chosen as the same-vendor adapter with the most VRAM, so nothing ties the two together on a two-Radeon machine. Whether that is a defect depends on Media Foundation and driver behaviour that cannot be checked here: whether MFTEnumEx returns one activate per adapter (each carrying MFT_ENUM_ADAPTER_LUID) and lists the iGPU's first, and whether the AMD MFT then refuses the other adapter's device at SET_D3D_MANAGER (a loud failure), does a cross-adapter copy, or just runs on whatever device it is given (no problem).
votes.reachable_by: Users with two GPUs of the same vendor (Ryzen APU + Radeon dGPU, Intel iGPU + Arc) on hardware encoders whose drivers register MFTs per adapter.
votes.fix_assessment: MFTEnum2 with MFT_ENUM_ADAPTER_LUID set from DXGI_ADAPTER_DESC1.AdapterLuid (gpu.rs already reads desc per adapter) is the documented way to tie the MFT to the device; keep MFTEnumEx as a fallback for systems where MFTEnum2 is unavailable.

title: fps choices up to panel refresh exceed H.264 Level 5.2 at 1440p/4K (S3)
claim: The fps choices go up to the panel's refresh (165/240). At 1440p/4K that exceeds H.264 Level 5.2 (1440p ≤ ~144 fps, 4K ≤ ~64 fps).
scenario: The MFT may refuse the media type or emit out-of-level streams.
fix: Not given explicitly in the report (implied: cap fps per resolution/level).

votes.evidence: src-tauri/src/capture.rs:598-606 `const STEPS = [30, 60, 120]; ... choices.push(refresh)` - fps up to panel refresh regardless of resolution; fit_to_target (capture.rs:641) only snaps fps to those steps. UI mirrors it: src/routes/Recording.tsx:14 `const HEIGHTS = [720, 1080, 1440, 2160]` and fpsChoices (Recording.tsx:27-30). Encoder sets only profile: mft.rs:780 `output.SetUINT32(&MF_MT_MPEG2_PROFILE, eAVEncH264VProfile_High...)`; no MF_MT_MPEG2_LEVEL / level anywhere (grep empty), and frame rate goes in as `MF_MT_FRAME_RATE` (mft.rs:523). A SetOutputType refusal propagates as Err 'Ausgabetyp: ...' (mft.rs:791-793). Arithmetic is right: Level 5.2 MaxMBPS 2,073,600 / 14,400 MB (1440p) = 144 fps; / 32,400 MB (2160p) = 64 fps.
votes.corrected_claim: Confirmed in code: 1440p at 165/240 and 2160p at 120/144+ can be configured, and no level is requested or capped. But Level 5.2 is not the top H.264 level (6.0-6.2 cover these rates), and since the app requests no level the MFT picks one itself. The outcome rests on driver behaviour not checkable here: a hardware MFT that auto-selects 6.x produces a valid stream (some hardware decoders may still reject it); one limited to 5.2 may refuse SetOutputType (recording fails loudly with 'Ausgabetyp') or mislabel the stream; and the encoder may simply lack the throughput.
votes.reachable_by: Users with 1440p >144 Hz or 4K >=120 Hz panels who pick the high fps option (the UI marks the refresh rate as '(source)').
votes.fix_assessment: Capping fps per resolution (or reading the encoder's supported level and frame-rate range) in fps_choices and the UI would prevent it, but it needs real-hardware evidence first; at minimum, log the level the encoder chose so field reports can tell.

title: No device-removed / encoder-death detection or recovery; errors only logged and a stale ring is saved as current
claim: Encoder failures are only logged: mft.rs:1312 and mft.rs:1344 are both `Err(err) => log::warn!("{err}")`; mft.rs:1174-1176 is `Disconnected => log::warn!("encoder has stopped — one frame is lost"); return false;`; the encoder thread exits quietly on event-queue errors (mft.rs:1284-1290). Nothing calls GetDeviceRemovedReason, and only `dropped` is counted (pipeline.rs:605-609). Shared::report() is only called on the capture path and only the first error per run is surfaced, so no banner appears and no restart happens.
scenario: A TDR or driver reset mid-game (also driver update, eGPU unplug, hybrid GPU switch): WGC stops delivering, the pacer repeats the last slot, the MFT fails or shuts down. The log gets ~60 warn lines per second and dropped climbs, but no banner appears. The ring keeps its pre-failure packets so 'Save clip' writes minutes-old footage as 'the last 30 s', or the ring silently fills with a frozen frame.
fix: Send encoder/D3D errors through Shared::report. Add a status-tick watchdog: no new packet for more than 2 s, or GetDeviceRemovedReason() != S_OK, reports and auto-restarts with a new device. Treat D2DERR_RECREATE_TARGET the same way, and flag saves whose newest packet is stale.

title: Recorder job queue is an unbounded std mpsc channel
claim: The recorder taps packets and audio blocks to its writer thread over `let (tx, rx) = channel::<Job>();` (recorder.rs:146), an unbounded std mpsc channel with no backpressure or fail policy.
scenario: A slow or sleeping HDD, NAS, USB drive or AV scan stalls the writer; video (~5 MB/s at 40 Mbit) plus PCM per source piles up in RAM indefinitely.
fix: Use a byte-bounded channel with an explicit fail-and-stop policy.

title: Recorder file I/O runs while holding the packet-ring and tracks locks
claim: pipeline.rs:954 takes `let ring = self.shared.packets.lock();` and Recorder::start (create_dir_all, File::create, meta write + rename, thread spawn) runs at pipeline.rs:964 while that lock is held. open_track (recorder.rs:306-322) writes meta.json from the mixer thread while holding shared.tracks.
scenario: Starting a recording on slow storage blocks the encoder's on_packet (which locks Shared.packets), so in_flight grows, submits wait or drop, and the NV12 slot-overwrite problem (VP-2) gets worse. Meta writes on slow disks stall the mixer.
fix: Do the file creation before taking the lock and only install the recorder under it. Move the meta writes into the writer thread.

title: Recording free-space guard ignores mix.pcm and stems, so finalize fails on long multi-source recordings
claim: The room guard is `if free < needed + RECORDING_SPARE_BYTES` with `needed = estimated mp4 size` (lib.rs:894-895). It does not account for finalize's sum_tracks writing mix.pcm (recorder.rs:580-583) or per-track stems.
scenario: A 2-hour recording with two or more main-mix sources: sum_tracks writes mix.pcm at ~691 MB/h, which the 512 MB spare can't cover. Finalize fails, the folder is kept, and it fails the same way on every start.
fix: Count mix PCM and stems in the guard, or skip pre-summing and let ffmpeg amix all the PCMs.

title: VideoProcessor auto-processing is not disabled, so driver enhancements may alter footage
claim: The VideoProcessor setup (convert.rs:141-168) only sets colour spaces; there is no `VideoProcessorSetStreamAutoProcessingMode(.., FALSE)`. Auto-processing is on by default.
scenario: Driver 'enhancement' features (sharpening, denoise, RTX video enhancement) may alter the captured footage.
fix: Disable auto-processing with VideoProcessorSetStreamAutoProcessingMode(.., FALSE).

title: VideoProcessor content description uses output size and sets no rects, so a resized window is stretched
claim: The content description in convert.rs:141-168 uses `InputWidth: width, InputHeight: height`, i.e. the output size rather than the source size, and no stream source/destination rectangle or background colour is set. The WGC frame pool is recreated on size change (wgc.rs:229-242) but window capture does not restart (state.rs:774).
scenario: A window resized after start is stretched to the fixed encoder size.
fix: Set stream source and destination rects that preserve aspect (letterbox) with a black background, and use the real source size in the content description.

title: ffmpeg/ffprobe runs have no timeout and no kill-on-close job object
claim: muxer::run uses `command.output()` (muxer.rs:65-68); run_reporting (muxer.rs:432-458) does `.stdout(Stdio::piped()).stderr(Stdio::piped()).spawn()` then `child.wait()`; ffprobe (muxer.rs:476-488) uses `.output()`. None has a timeout/kill, and children are not placed in a job object with KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE.
scenario: A network share vanishes mid-write: ffmpeg blocks forever, SavingGuard stays set, and every later save says 'already being saved' until restart. A crash during a save leaves an orphaned ffmpeg process.
fix: Put ffmpeg/ffprobe in a job object with KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE; wait with a timeout and kill.

also.title: No cancel, timeout or kill for ffmpeg, and it runs at normal priority next to the game
also.claim: The ffmpeg runner in edit.rs:749-796 (and the muxer's `run`) has no Job Object, `kill`, `try_wait` or timeout anywhere in the crate (grep-confirmed). A hung hardware encoder holds `edit::WORKING` forever; on app exit ffmpeg children are orphaned (Windows does not kill children); x264 `-preset medium` exports started from the in-game console compete with the game at normal priority.
also.fix: Put children in a Job Object with `JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE`; use `BELOW_NORMAL_PRIORITY_CLASS`; add a cancel token that kills the child and a stall watchdog when `out_time` stops advancing; consider `-hwaccel d3d11va` for decoding.

title: ffmpeg inherits the parent's stdin (no Stdio::null, no -nostdin)
claim: run_reporting (muxer.rs:432-458) spawns ffmpeg with piped stdout/stderr but no stdin setting and without `-nostdin`, so stdin is inherited.
scenario: When the app is started from a console, ffmpeg reads that console's stdin.
fix: Use Stdio::null() for stdin plus -nostdin.

title: Orphaned .part.mp4 files in the clip folder are never cleaned up
claim: The in-progress output `<stem>_<id>.part.mp4` is written beside the target clip (muxer.rs:323), but the startup leftover cleanup (lib.rs:677-688) only cleans data_dir/temp.
scenario: A crash during a save leaves a `<stem>_<id>.part.mp4` in the user's clip folder forever.
fix: Sweep stale *.part.mp4 at startup.

also.title: Temp files litter the user's clip folder after a crash
also.claim: Edit temp files `*.{pid}.neu.mp4` (edit.rs:422) and export files `"{stem} (N MB).mp4"` are written into the user's clip folder and are never cleaned up after a crash.
also.fix: No explicit fix given; implied: clean up stale temp files (e.g. in `repair`).

title: Closed or recreated window is never recovered during window capture
claim: The WGC Closed handler only sets a flag and reports once (pipeline.rs:689-695). Drift detection returns None for windows: `|| config.target_kind != TargetKind::Monitor` (state.rs:772-776), so nothing restarts or re-targets capture.
scenario: The game window closes or restarts with a new HWND. After one banner, the buffer encodes the last frame forever.
fix: Stop the buffer, or re-resolve the window by process and restart.

title: halt_pipeline holds the pipeline mutex during the stop
claim: state.rs:559-561 is `if let Some(mut pipeline) = self.pipeline.lock().take() { pipeline.stop(); }`; under Rust 2021 the temporary lock guard lives across stop().
scenario: is_buffering, save and start callers block for up to the 2 s drain.
fix: Bind the take() result to a local first.

also.title: halt_pipeline holds the pipeline lock during the whole Pipeline::stop
also.claim: state.rs:559: `if let Some(mut pipeline) = self.pipeline.lock().take() { pipeline.stop(); }`. In edition 2021 the guard temporary lives through the whole `if let`, so the `pipeline` mutex is held across `Pipeline::stop`'s joins (the entire encoder drain).
also.fix: `let p = self.pipeline.lock().take(); if let Some(mut p) = p { p.stop(); }`

title: Hardware MFT is never shut down (no IMFShutdown / ShutdownObject / SET_D3D_MANAGER(0))
claim: The MFT is created by `candidates[pick].activate.ActivateObject()` (mft.rs:716) and the IMFActivate is dropped at the end of build. The run ends with only `ProcessMessage(MFT_MESSAGE_NOTIFY_END_STREAMING, 0)` (mft.rs:1440-1444). There is no IMFShutdown::Shutdown, no IMFActivate::ShutdownObject, and no MFT_MESSAGE_SET_D3D_MANAGER(0). Media Foundation makes the caller of ActivateObject responsible for shutdown, and async MFTs own event queues and worker threads.
scenario: Some vendor MFTs keep the encoder session, device manager and D3D device alive. Each buffer restart can leak an NVENC/AMF session until the consumer session cap is hit and 'Buffer will not start' appears, along with VRAM growth.
fix: Store the activate object. After the drain: SET_D3D_MANAGER(0), then cast::<IMFShutdown>()?.Shutdown(), then activate.ShutdownObject(). Send MFT_MESSAGE_NOTIFY_END_OF_STREAM before COMMAND_DRAIN.

title: Replay ring length and byte limits are not enforced when only one keyframe exists
claim: Trimming in the ReplayBuffer only runs `while self.keyframes.len() > 1 {` (buffer.rs:93), and the no-keyframe safety net returns early with `if !self.keyframes.is_empty() || self.packets.is_empty() { return; }` (buffer.rs:128). With exactly one keyframe neither the pts-length nor the byte-budget limit applies and the safety net is skipped, so the ring grows without bound. The GOP read-back from the encoder is only logged. Existing tests only cover zero or many keyframes.
scenario: An encoder ignores the GOP setting (infinite GOP or intra-refresh) and sends only its initial IDR; the ring grows until OOM. (Report: the logic is confirmed, the trigger is speculative.)
fix: If no keyframe arrives within 2× GOP, force one (CODECAPI_AVEncVideoForceKeyFrame). When over budget with a single GOP, drop the ring and wait for the next IDR (memory should win, as the module's own doc says). Add a unit test for the single-keyframe case.

title: sum_tracks duplicates write_mix_wav
claim: recorder::sum_tracks duplicates the mixing logic of write_mix_wav.
scenario: Duplicate mixing code that can diverge.
fix: Not given explicitly in the report (implied: share one implementation).

votes.evidence: src-tauri/src/pipeline.rs:222-234 write_mix_wav: allocates `vec![0i16; frames * CHANNELS]`, sums `track.window(from_100ns, frames)` from the in-memory TrackRings, then `write_wav(path, &sum)` (with a RIFF header). src-tauri/src/recorder.rs:453-485 sum_tracks: opens the files, streams 64 KiB blocks through `read_full`, tracks `longest` per block, and writes headerless PCM through a BufWriter. Its doc comment gives the reason it is separate: "block by block — an hour of audio per source does not go through memory in one piece. Saturating, like `pipeline::write_mix_wav`". The only code in common is the one expression `*slot = slot.saturating_add(sample)` (pipeline.rs:230 vs recorder.rs:476).
votes.corrected_claim: The two functions share only the one-line rule for combining samples (a saturating i16 add), and the code cross-references it on purpose. Everything else differs, and has to: the sources (TrackRing windows in memory vs PCM files streamed from disk), the output (a WAV with a header vs raw PCM), and the length rule (a fixed frame count vs the longest input). That is not duplicated mixing logic.
votes.reachable_by: Nothing at runtime. At most, a maintainer who changes the saturation policy has to touch two one-liners. The doc comment already points from one to the other.
votes.fix_assessment: "Share one implementation" is not practical without forcing in-memory rings and streamed files behind one abstraction. At most, a 3-line `fn mix_into(dst: &mut [i16], src: impl Iterator<Item=i16>)` helper could be shared, and that gains almost nothing.
